nameStory: This jellyfish gets its "lion's mane" name from the flowing, hair-like tentacles that stream beneath its bell, resembling the magnificent mane of a lion flowing in the wind. The "Atlantic" part of its name distinguishes it from its larger Arctic cousin, since this species prefers the warmer waters along the Mid-Atlantic coast.
description: The Atlantic Lion's Mane Jelly is a medium-sized jellyfish that drifts through New England's coastal waters like a translucent underwater parachute. These jellies typically measure about two inches across their bell-shaped body, making them smaller than their famous giant cousin but still substantial enough to notice. Their most striking feature is the cluster of flowing tentacles beneath their body, along with four distinctive mouth-parts that have a warm cinnamon color with a darker center.

idTips.label: Four Cinnamon Mouth-Parts
idTips.description: Look for four ribbon-like mouth tentacles with a distinctive cinnamon or rust color and darker centers - these are the key identifying feature that distinguishes mature Atlantic Lion's Mane jellies from other species

idTips.label: Two-Inch Bell Size
idTips.description: The bell measures roughly two inches across - about the size of a tennis ball when fully expanded, making it noticeably smaller than the giant Lion's Mane but larger than the tiny Dwarf Lion's Mane

idTips.label: Moderate Fold Pattern
idTips.description: The bell has thin, delicate folds around its margin that are more numerous than the Dwarf Lion's Mane but fewer than the Arctic Lion's Mane - these folds feel remarkably thin and fragile

idTips.label: Flowing Hair-like Tentacles
idTips.description: Streaming tentacles beneath the bell move like underwater hair in the current, creating the characteristic "mane" appearance that gives this jelly its name

idTips.label: Moderate Sting
idTips.description: If accidentally touched, produces only a moderate burning sensation rather than the intense pain of some other jellyfish - though you should still avoid contact

habitat: These jellies prefer the shallower coastal waters south of Cape Cod, making them common visitors to beaches and bays along southern New England. They're especially abundant in protected areas like Long Island Sound, where the water is calmer and slightly warmer than the open ocean.

seasonality.spring: Young jellies may start appearing in late spring as water temperatures warm, though they're still developing their full complement of tentacles and mouth-parts.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Atlantic Lion's Mane jellies, when they reach their full size and distinctive cinnamon coloring is most pronounced in mid-summer warmth.
seasonality.fall: Numbers begin to decline as water temperatures cool, though some individuals may persist into early fall in protected bays.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters during the cold months, as they cannot survive the winter temperatures.

funFact: These jellies are microscopic weapons factories - they produce more different types of stinging cells (called nematocysts) than almost any other jellyfish, including some that are longer on average than those of other common species!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its larger cousin, the Giant Lion's Mane Jelly, but remember "Atlantic-sized" means tennis ball-sized (2 inches), while the giant can be dinner plate-sized or larger. The cinnamon-colored mouth tentacles are your best clue - count four of them to confirm you've found an Atlantic Lion's Mane.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the "Atlantic" Lion's Mane, this species is actually more limited in range than its name suggests, preferring the warmer Mid-Atlantic waters rather than the entire Atlantic coast. Many scientists consider it a warm-water variety of the more widespread Lion's Mane Jelly rather than a completely separate species.
compareHints: Within the Lion's Mane family, the Atlantic species sits right in the middle size-wise - bigger than the tiny Dwarf Lion's Mane but much smaller than the Giant Lion's Mane that can grow huge in colder northern waters. The Atlantic species also has fewer bell folds than the Giant but more than the Dwarf, making it the "Goldilocks" of the lion's mane jellies. The warm cinnamon coloring of the mouth-parts is also more pronounced than in its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The dwarf lion's mane is significantly smaller than the giant lion's mane jelly (Cyanea capillata), which can have bells several feet across.
The Lion's Mane Jelly is much larger than its relatives, the Atlantic Lion's Mane Jelly and Dwarf Lion's Mane Jelly.
